explanations.answer: Welcome her and help with anything she needs
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Paul says, "Welcome her in the Lord in a manner worthy of the saints, and assist her with anything she may need from you." Phoebe is a servant of the church in Cenchrea, and Paul wants her treated right. Whatever she needs, the believers in Rome are to pitch in. That's a good rule for any kitchen, too.

explanations.answer: Send her straight on to Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Close to a travel plan, but the verse doesn't say anything about Jerusalem. Paul asks the believers in Rome to welcome Phoebe and to assist her with anything she may need from them. Phoebe is a servant of the church in Cenchrea, and this is how Paul introduces her. The ask is a warm welcome and real help, and no sending her anywhere.

explanations.answer: Find her a ship headed for Spain
explanations.explanation: I love the creativity, friend, but there's no ship in this verse. Paul says to welcome Phoebe in a manner worthy of the saints and to assist her with anything she may need. Phoebe is a servant of the church in Cenchrea. Nothing is said about where she's going next, only that she's to be welcomed and helped.

Careful, friend, because Paul says it bigger than that. He says Phoebe "has been a great help to many people, including me." Look at that little word "many." Paul is one of a whole line of folks she has helped, and he's glad to say so.

That's right, baker. Paul says Phoebe "has been a great help to many people, including me." So Paul is one of many people she has helped. That's a servant of the church in Cenchrea for you, and her helping reaches well past one man.

You got it, baker. Paul says to watch out for those who create divisions and obstacles contrary to the teaching they have learned, and then he adds, "Turn away from them." It's short and it's plain. When I'm holding a hot tray, I don't need a second opinion on where to point my mustache.

That sounds like a lot of work, friend, and Paul never asks for it. His instruction is just three words: "Turn away from them." He says it about those who create divisions and obstacles contrary to the teaching the believers had learned. A public debate isn't in the verse at all.

That's a reasonable-sounding idea, but it isn't what Paul writes. He says to watch out for the people who create divisions and obstacles contrary to the teaching they have learned. Then comes his instruction: "Turn away from them." The elders aren't mentioned anywhere in this passage.

Yes, baker. Paul says such people "are not serving our Lord Christ, but their own appetites." Their hearts are pointed at what they want. Believe me, I know the pull of an appetite. A fresh batch of cookies cooling on the rack has tested me more than once.

Reputations sound believable, friend, but Paul doesn't say that. He says they're not serving our Lord Christ, "but their own appetites." That's the word he picks. I'd rather stick with what he actually wrote.

That one would be a surprise, baker, because serving a family is a fine thing to do. Paul says something different about these people. They're not serving our Lord Christ, "but their own appetites." Families don't come up in that verse at all.

Not quite, friend. Paul never mentions loud threats. He says that "By smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive." It's the quiet, friendly voice that does the fooling, so a pleasant tone doesn't prove a person is safe.

That's right, baker. Paul says, "By smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the naive." There's no shouting or threatening in the verse. The danger he describes is sweet words that sound nice.

explanations.answer: Everyone has heard about their obedience
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul writes, "Everyone has heard about your obedience, so I rejoice over you." The news about the believers in Rome had spread. Paul heard it, and it made him glad. Imagine your good name traveling farther than you do.

explanations.answer: Their church has grown so quickly
explanations.explanation: Growth would be good news, friend, but Paul doesn't say that here. His reason is, "Everyone has heard about your obedience, so I rejoice over you." The verse says nothing about how fast the church has grown. What he celebrates is their obedience, and that word has gotten around.

explanations.answer: They have sent him a generous gift
explanations.explanation: That's a nice thought, baker, but no gift shows up in this verse. Paul gives his reason plainly: "Everyone has heard about your obedience, so I rejoice over you." What makes him glad is their obedience, and everyone has heard about it.

That's it, baker. Paul says, "But I want you to be wise about what is good and innocent about what is evil." So he wants them wise about the good and innocent about the evil. That's a lot like handling dough. I'll be a pro at the good part, and the burnt part I don't need to know a thing about.

Popular is a fun guess, friend, but it's not Paul's word. He says, "But I want you to be wise about what is good and innocent about what is evil." What's popular doesn't come into it. What matters to him is good and evil.

Interesting guess, baker, but Paul isn't talking about anything foreign. He says, "But I want you to be wise about what is good and innocent about what is evil." The word he uses is "evil." Good on one side, evil on the other.

True, baker. Paul says, "The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet." The one doing the crushing is the God of peace. I'll tell you, I find that comforting. I spent years in the dark, and I know a promise like that hits different.

Actually, baker, Paul really does say it. His words are, "The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet." It's God who does the crushing, and Paul says it will be soon. Good thing it's right there in the verse.

explanations.answer: The one who wrote down this letter
explanations.explanation: That's him, baker. Tertius says it himself: "I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord." When he writes "I," it's his own voice breaking into Paul's letter. He gets his own greeting, and he earned it.

explanations.answer: The one who will carry this letter
explanations.explanation: Good guess, friend, but the verse doesn't say that. Tertius calls himself the one "who wrote down this letter." Nothing in this passage tells us who carries it. What Tertius tells us about himself is that he wrote it down.

explanations.answer: The leader of the church in Rome
explanations.explanation: That's a bit off, baker. Tertius is sending greetings to the believers in Rome, so he isn't leading them. He says, "I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord." His job is the writing.
You got it, baker. Paul says Gaius "has hosted me and all the church." That's the whole church at his place. I can barely handle a few bakers crowding my counter, so I'm impressed.

A meeting hall would be impressive, friend, but the verse never says Gaius built one. What it says is that Gaius "has hosted me and all the church." He's known for making room for them, Paul included. The building isn't mentioned.
Not this time, baker. Ephesus doesn't appear in this verse, and neither does teaching. Paul says Gaius "has hosted me and all the church." That's his claim to fame here.

Not quite, baker. Paul calls it "the revelation of the mystery concealed for ages past" (Romans 16:25). Then he goes on to say it is "now revealed and made known through the writings of the prophets." It was concealed for ages past, but it isn't staying that way.

That's right, baker. Paul says the mystery was "concealed for ages past but now revealed and made known through the writings of the prophets" (Romans 16:25-26). The key word is "now." What was hidden has been made known, so it's out of the oven and on the table.

Yes, baker. Paul says the mystery is made known "in order to lead all nations to the obedience that comes from faith." Not just one nation, but all of them. That's a big guest list, and I'd need a lot of cookie boxes.
Priests are a fair guess, friend, but that's not Paul's word. He says it's "in order to lead all nations to the obedience that comes from faith." The word is "nations," and he says "all" of them.

Elders sound sensible, baker, but Paul doesn't say elders here. The verse says it is "in order to lead all nations to the obedience that comes from faith." The word is "nations." He said "all," and he meant all.

That's the one, baker. Paul closes with, "to the only wise God be glory forever through Jesus Christ! Amen." That's how he ends the whole letter, with glory to God forever through Jesus Christ. It's a mighty good last line.

Angels are a fair guess, friend, but they're not in this verse. Paul says, "to the only wise God be glory forever through Jesus Christ! Amen." The name he lands on is Jesus Christ. That's how the letter ends.

That's close to home for Paul, since he's an apostle himself, but it isn't his answer. He ends with, "to the only wise God be glory forever through Jesus Christ! Amen." It's Jesus Christ he names. So the apostles don't make it into that final line.
